title: Fossils in the schist
teaches: How the conditions a rock has been through sort it into one of three families, and why the families shade into one another

parts.title: The oldest rocks in the world

blocks.text: In the 1780s the most influential teacher of geology in Europe was Abraham Gottlob Werner, at the mining academy in Freiberg, Saxony, whose followers thought basalt had settled out of the sea (lesson 4). Students came from across the continent to hear him, and they went home with his way of sorting rocks. Werner sorted them by age. At the bottom of every mountain range, he taught, lay the **Primitive** rocks: granite, gneiss, mica schist, slate and a crystalline white limestone. They were hard, glittering with crystals, and held no fossils, so they must have formed first, before anything lived. Above them came rocks with a few fossils, then the soft, layered, fossil-rich beds of the lowlands, and finally loose gravel and sand.

The scheme was tidy, and it was useful to miners, who could learn what lay under what. Its trouble was that rocks kept turning up in the wrong drawer. Lesson 4 described one problem: granite that had been squeezed, molten, into cracks in younger rock. A second came from the Alps. By the 1820s and 1830s geologists working there were finding glittering, crystalline schists and marbles that could be followed along the mountainside into ordinary shale and limestone with fossils in them. In some places the schist held fossils itself: **belemnites**, the bullet-shaped internal shells of squid-like animals that lived in the Jurassic seas, stretched and snapped apart inside rock that Werner would have called Primitive.

A fossil cannot be older than life, so these "Primitive" schists were not primitive at all. They were sea-floor mud and lime that had become schist and marble long after the belemnites died in them. The rocks of lesson 5 had made the same point in Scotland, where beds of mud could be traced on foot into garnet schist. What a rock looks like does not say when it formed. It says what has happened to it.

In 1833, in the third volume of his *Principles of Geology*, Charles Lyell gave such rocks a name: **metamorphic**, from the Greek for "change of form". A few years later he sorted all rocks into three families by how they had formed rather than by age, and the scheme has lasted. Rocks laid down at the surface from sediment are **sedimentary**. Rocks that cooled from a melt are **igneous**. Rocks changed in the solid state by heat and pressure are metamorphic. Each family can form at any time in the Earth's history, and a single rock can pass from one family to another.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Werner sorted rocks by supposed age; crystalline schists and marbles were "Primitive", formed before life.
Fossils in Alpine schists, and mud beds traced into schist, showed that crystalline rocks can be altered sediment.
Lyell named metamorphic rocks in 1833. Rocks are now sorted by how they formed: sedimentary, igneous, metamorphic.

parts.title: Three ways to make a rock

blocks.text: Each family is defined by the conditions a rock met. A **sedimentary** rock forms at or near the surface, where temperatures stay below roughly 200 °C (the line is approximate, as the next part shows). Some sedimentary rocks are made of broken pieces of older rock, named by the size of the pieces: conglomerate from pebbles, sandstone from sand, shale and mudstone from mud. Others are made of what water and living things drop out of solution, such as limestone from shells and lime mud, or rock salt from an evaporating sea. Either way, the weight of later layers presses the sediment together, minerals left by water seeping through it glue the grains, and it becomes rock; the rock keeps a record of where it was laid down: a river, a beach, a dune field (lesson 2), a reef or the deep sea floor.

Above roughly 200 °C, buried rock begins to recrystallise without melting, as in lesson 5. It is now **metamorphic**. Rocks made of many minerals grow new ones, and under a squeeze their flat minerals line up, so they are named mostly by texture: slate, schist, gneiss. Rocks made of a single mineral have nothing new to grow, so their crystals simply grow larger and lock together: sandstone of nearly pure quartz becomes **quartzite**, and limestone becomes **marble**. Heat it further and a rock begins to melt; once it has melted and cooled again, it is **igneous**, named by its grain size and what the melt was made of (lesson 4).

The chart below puts a rock through any depth and temperature. The dashed line is the usual warming with depth in continental crust, about 25 °C per kilometre. Where a rock lands off that line, something unusual is going on: hot and shallow beside a body of magma, or cold and deep where one plate dives under another, which makes the blueschist of lesson 5 (the blue corner of the chart).

blocks.caption: Depth down, temperature across. Pick a starting rock, then drag the dot. The shaded bands show what that rock does in each range of temperature.
blocks.task: Guess first, then take the mudstone deep and hot enough to start melting

blocks.text: Granite and mudstone start to melt at about 650 to 700 °C when there is some water in the rock, as there nearly always is. Wet basalt needs about 800 to 850 °C to start (dry basalt over 1,000 °C) and about 1,200 °C to melt through. A rock of one pure mineral holds out far longer than a mixture: quartz on its own melts only above about 1,700 °C, and calcite under pressure above 1,300 °C, both far hotter than the crust ever gets. So pure quartz sandstone and limestone stay quartzite and marble. Which rock melts first depends on what it is made of, a point the last part of this lesson comes back to.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Sedimentary rocks form at or near the surface, below about 200 °C, and record how and where their sediment was laid down.
Metamorphic rocks recrystallise in the solid state, from about 200 °C up to the start of melting; single-mineral rocks become quartzite and marble.
Igneous rocks cool from a melt. Granite and mud melt at much lower temperatures than basalt.

blocks.text: Move the dot slowly and the families stop looking like boxes. Buried mud becomes mudstone or shale, still sedimentary; heated further it becomes slate, then **phyllite** (slate whose flakes have grown big enough to shine), then schist and gneiss, each grading into the next with no sharp break. Geologists draw the line between sedimentary and metamorphic at around 200 °C, but a mudstone at 180 °C and a slate at 220 °C are close kin, and their boundary is a matter of convention. The same is true at the hot end. Past about 650 to 700 °C the pale minerals in a gneiss begin to melt while the dark ones stay solid, and the rock that results is called **migmatite**, Greek for "mixed rock": part metamorphic, with streaks and pods of what is already granite.

blocks.caption: Gneiss, with pale and dark minerals sorted into bands. A little hotter, and the pale bands would start to melt.

blocks.text: The families blur at the surface too. Volcanic ash is igneous material, but it falls out of the sky and settles in layers like any sediment, so the rock it makes, **tuff**, belongs to both. Granite that weathers in place falls apart into grains of quartz and feldspar, and a river can carry them a few kilometres and drop them as sand that hardens into sandstone made almost entirely of granite. Because it is still made of quartz and feldspar, not quartz alone, bury and heat that sandstone and it becomes a gneiss that a geologist can hardly tell from the gneiss made from the original granite.

Many rock names therefore describe a stage rather than a material. Mud, shale, slate, schist, gneiss, migmatite and granite can be much the same material at different moments, and the name records what it has been through: how deep it was buried, how hot it got, and how long it stayed there.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The families grade into one another: mudstone to shale, slate, phyllite, schist, gneiss, then migmatite as melting begins.
Tuff is volcanic and sedimentary at once; granite can weather into sand that becomes sandstone, then gneiss.
A rock's name records the conditions it went through more than what it is made of.

blocks.text: Igneous rocks are sorted on the two axes lesson 4 introduced. One is how fast the melt cooled, which sets the grain size: fine grains or glass for lava chilled at the surface, coarse crystals for magma that cooled slowly underground. The other is what the melt was made of. Melts rich in silica crystallise to pale quartz and feldspar; melts poorer in silica and richer in iron and magnesium crystallise to dark minerals. Six common names cover most of the grid: rhyolite, andesite and basalt for the fine-grained rocks, and granite, diorite and gabbro for the coarse ones. **Andesite**, named after the Andes, and **dacite**, a little richer in silica, are the in-between lavas of volcanoes like those of the Andes and the Cascades.

blocks.caption: The common igneous rocks, by how fast they cooled (down) and what the melt was made of (across). Each pair in a column is the same melt.
Granite: the coarse, slowly cooled form of a silica-rich melt. Erupted, the same melt makes rhyolite, pumice or obsidian.

blocks.text: Each column holds one melt in two forms. Granite and rhyolite are the same melt, one cooled deep and one erupted; gabbro and basalt are the same, too. Geologists refine the grid when they need precision. For coarse rocks they count the proportions of quartz, alkali feldspar, plagioclase feldspar and the rarer feldspathoids, and plot them on a pair of triangles called the **QAPF** diagram after those four letters. For fine-grained rocks, whose crystals are too small to count, they analyse the chemistry and plot sodium plus potassium against silica, the **TAS** diagram (total alkalis against silica). Both are finer cuts across the same silica axis.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Igneous rocks are named by cooling rate (fine or coarse) and by silica content (pale or dark).
Each fine-grained rock has a coarse-grained twin made from the same melt: rhyolite and granite, andesite and diorite, basalt and gabbro.

blocks.text: In the 1910s and 1920s Norman Bowen, a Canadian working at the Geophysical Laboratory in Washington, D.C., showed why a melt can become rich in silica, and why granite melts so much more easily than basalt. He melted mixtures of rock-forming minerals in small capsules, cooled them to a set temperature, and then quenched them in water or mercury so that whatever crystals had formed by then were frozen in place in glass. Run after run, the crystals appeared in the same order.

blocks.caption: Bowen's order, for a basalt melt cooling slowly. Left, the minerals as they appear; right, a magma chamber where each crystal settles to the floor as it forms.
blocks.task: Cool the melt until the last mineral crystallises

blocks.text: The first crystals out of a basalt melt are olivine and calcium-rich feldspar, minerals poor in silica. If they sink out of the liquid, what remains is richer in silica. Cool it further and it would erupt as andesite, then dacite, and finally rhyolite. A single magma can therefore give rise to a whole family of related igneous rocks, depending on how much of the melt had crystallised before the rest escaped from the chamber. This process, **fractional crystallisation**, is one of the main reasons different volcanoes, and different eruptions of one volcano, produce different lavas.

The order also works backwards. The minerals that crystallise last, at the lowest temperatures, are the first to melt when a rock is heated: quartz, potassium feldspar and mica. Those are what granite, and mud that has become gneiss, are mostly made of. That is why they start to melt at about 650 to 700 °C while basalt holds out to 800 °C or more, and why the first melt of the thick, light crust under the continents usually has the make-up of granite. The pale veins in a migmatite are that first melt.

The order even reaches the surface. In 1938 Samuel Goldich showed that minerals weather in roughly the same sequence: those that formed hottest, such as olivine, break down fastest in rain and soil, and quartz, which formed coolest, barely breaks down at all. Feldspar rots to clay. So a weathered granite leaves quartz sand and clay mud, the raw material for sandstone and shale, and the sand on most beaches is mostly quartz. One sequence of minerals links the igneous rocks to the sediments made from them and to the metamorphic rocks that melt back into granite.

What carries a rock from one family to the next, again and again, is a loop now called the rock cycle. At a headland on the Scottish coast James Hutton saw two turns of it in a single cliff, and asked how long they had taken.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Bowen found that minerals crystallise from a cooling melt in a fixed order: olivine and calcium feldspar first, quartz last.
Removing early crystals makes the remaining melt richer in silica, so one magma can produce basalt, andesite, dacite and rhyolite.
Minerals that crystallise last melt first, so the first melt of continental crust is granite-like; weathering follows the same order, leaving quartz sand and clay.

blocks.caption: Six questions on the three families of rock
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Werner taught that schist was Primitive, older than life. Why did belemnites found inside Alpine schist matter?
choices: The schist must have been sediment, laid down after those animals lived, then changed
Belemnites must have lived much earlier than anyone had thought
The fossils must have been carried into the schist later by groundwater
items.why: A fossil cannot be older than the animal it came from. Schist holding Jurassic belemnites began as Jurassic sea-floor sediment and became schist afterwards: it is metamorphic.

items.ask: This is shale. It is buried about 20 km down, where it reaches about 500 °C, and stays solid. What does it most likely become?
items.why: Slate forms at lower temperatures, from about 200 °C. At around 500 °C mica and garnet grow into schist. Migmatite needs partial melting, above about 650 to 700 °C.

items.ask: A bed of limestone packed with fossil shells is buried and heated to 600 °C. What happens to the fossils?
choices: They vanish as the calcite regrows into interlocking crystals
They survive unchanged, because limestone does not melt in the crust
items.why: Limestone does not melt at 600 °C, but it does recrystallise: the calcite of shells and mud regrows as an even mosaic of crystals, which is marble, and the fossils are wiped out.

items.ask: This rhyolite and a granite have nearly the same chemistry. Why do they look so different?
choices: The rhyolite cooled quickly at the surface; the granite cooled slowly underground
The rhyolite was heated and squeezed after it formed
The granite formed from a melt with much more iron and magnesium
items.why: They are one silica-rich melt in two forms. Fast cooling gives fine grains or glass; slow cooling gives coarse crystals.

items.ask: Granite and basalt are heated side by side deep in the crust. Granite starts to melt at about 650 to 700 °C, basalt only at 800 °C or higher. Why?
choices: Granite is mostly quartz, feldspar and mica, the minerals that crystallise last from a melt
Granite holds more olivine and pyroxene, which melt easily
Basalt cooled faster, so its crystals are smaller and harder to melt
items.why: Bowen's order run backwards: the minerals that crystallise at the lowest temperatures are the first to melt. Olivine and pyroxene crystallise first and melt last.

items.ask: A granite hillside weathers for a very long time. Which mineral is most likely to survive as grains for a river to carry away?
items.why: Quartz, the last mineral to crystallise, barely weathers, so it survives as sand. Feldspar rots to clay, and biotite breaks down too.

summary: **Rocks are sorted by how they formed, not by age.** Fossils in Alpine schists and Scottish mud traced into schist ended Werner's scheme of "Primitive" rocks; Lyell named metamorphic rocks in 1833.
**Sedimentary rocks form at the surface.** They are made of pieces of older rock or of what water and living things drop, cemented below about 200 °C, and they record where they were laid down.
**Metamorphic rocks recrystallise without melting.** From about 200 °C to the start of melting, mud becomes slate, schist and gneiss; sandstone becomes quartzite and limestone marble.
**Igneous rocks cool from a melt.** They are named by grain size (cooling rate) and silica content; rhyolite and granite, basalt and gabbro are the same melts cooled fast or slowly.
**The families grade into one another.** Migmatite is part metamorphic, part granite; tuff is volcanic and sedimentary; a rock's name records what it went through.

**Bowen's order ties them together.** Minerals crystallise from olivine to quartz; removing early crystals makes a melt richer in silica, the last to crystallise melt first, and weathering leaves quartz sand and clay.
